# The Light-Leak

The camera arrived in a shoebox, wrapped in a dish towel that smelled faintly of lavender and cigarettes. Mrs. Okonkwo pressed it into my hands on the Thursday before the Maple Street block party like she was handing over a sleeping infant.

"It was my husband's," she said. "A Yashica Mat, 1968. He photographed every wedding on this block for thirty years. I haven't touched it since he passed."

I had volunteered to document the party for the neighborhood association's newsletter—mostly because I'd mentioned at the last meeting that I "liked photography," which was technically true. I liked the idea of it. I owned a phone like everyone else and had once done a mediocre job shooting my cousin's engagement photos. But the newsletter needed pictures, and I'd opened my mouth, and now I was holding sixty-year-old machinery I didn't understand.

"It's fully manual," Mrs. Okonkwo said, watching me turn it over. "You'll have to learn the exposure. Sunny sixteen."

"Sunny what?"

She laughed—a short, surprised sound, like she hadn't expected to. "Come by tomorrow. I'll show you."
